newsitem.title: UK: Regan says advice to Galileo on CWS bid was inept.
newsitem.headline: Regan says advice to Galileo on CWS bid was inept.

text.p: Andrew Regan, the entrepreneur behind the failed bid for Britain's Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS), said on Thursday the advice given to his Galileo bidding vehicle was inept.
The statement came only hours after Galileo's advisor Hambros admitted that its role in the failed bid fell short of good busines practice.

"The events of this week make it perfectly clear that the advice Galileo paid so many millions of pounds for, and followed every inch of the way, was inept," Regan said in a statement, adding he was "delighted that the true story" was emerging.

"I always believed I could rely on my City advisers, but the unpublished Norton Rose report obviously shows that I was wrong to do so. I, and Galileo's other investors, still await an apology from those who took Galileo's money so readily," he added.

Earlier British investment bank Hambros parted ways with three of its bankers, including corporate finance head Nigel Pantling, after the independent Norton Rose probe into its role found the conduct of those involved, while without dishonest intent, "fell well short of the standards of good business practice".

City watchdog The Securities and Futures Authority (SFA) said it would study the report, which has also been passed to the Bank of England, and decide whether it needed to undertake its own inquiry or take action against Hambros or the individuals concerned.

On Tuesday Nigel Campion-Smith, the lawyer who acted for Regan, resigned as a partner at City law firm Travers Smith Braithwaite because he felt responsible for the embarrassment the CWS affair had caused to the firm.

Regan's audacious 1.2 billion pound ($2 billion) takeover attempt of mutually-owned supermarkets-to-funeral parlours group CWS collapsed in April after sustained legal action by the Co-op and the withdrawal of key financial backing for the bid. ($ = 0.593 British Pounds)
